Frequency-Domain #transfer-function
For a continuous-time linear time-invariant system with zero initial conditions, let $G(s)$ be the forward path and $H(s)$ the feedback path. Negative feedback means $E(s)=R(s)-H(s)Y(s)$. Substituting $Y(s)=G(s)E(s)$ gives
$$\frac{Y(s)}{R(s)}=\frac{G(s)}{1+G(s)H(s)}.$$
The formula describes the loop even when it is unstable; check stability before taking a final value.

See this for applications
$A$ proper rational continuous-time transfer function is BIBO stable when every pole of its reduced form has strictly negative real part. For a state-space model, asymptotic internal stability requires every eigenvalue of A to satisfy that condition. A canceled pole can hide an unstable internal mode.1

Time response

Tip 

For a stable first-order model $G(s)=K/(\tau s+1)$ with $\tau>0$, zero initial conditions, and no delay, an input step of amplitude $A$ gives $y(t)=KA(1-e^{-t/\tau})$ for $t\geq0$. The response reaches $1-e^{-1}\approx63.2\%$ of its final change at $t=\tau$. Read $K=y(\infty)/A$ from the final value and $\tau$ from that crossing. This rule assumes the first-order model fits the graph.2

Time-response #os-percent-overshoot
steady-state error
With unity negative feedback and zero initial conditions, let $G(s)$ include the controller and plant. Then
$$\begin{aligned}
Y(s) &= E(s)G(s) \\
E(s) &= R(s) - Y(s)
\end{aligned}$$
so $E(s)/R(s)=1/(1+G(s))$. This holds for a dynamic $G(s)$ as well as a constant gain. To use $e_{\mathrm{ss}}=\lim_{s\to0}sE(s)$, check that every pole of the reduced expression $sE(s)$ has strictly negative real part. See the steady-state error derivation for the input-specific limits.
state space design
Pole placement with phase-variable form
With full-state feedback $u=-Kx$, the state equation becomes $\dot{x}=(A-BK)x$. Its characteristic equation is
$$\det\!\left(sI-(A-BK)\right)=0.$$
Arbitrary pole placement requires $(A,B)$ to be controllable. For a real model, choose complex poles in conjugate pairs. In controller canonical form, match the coefficients of this determinant to the polynomial formed from the desired poles.3
Placing a pole at $s=-2$ cancels a zero only when the same transfer function’s numerator contains the factor $s+2$. Check the full state model before simplifying: the canceled mode still exists internally.1
Gain and Phase Stability Margins
For scalar loop transfer $L(s)=KG(s)H(s)$ with negative feedback, the characteristic equation is
$$1+KG(s)H(s) = 0.$$
Clear the transfer-function denominators to obtain the characteristic polynomial. At a phase crossover $\arg L(j\omega_{\mathrm{pc}})=-180^\circ$, the gain margin is $1/|L(j\omega_{\mathrm{pc}})|$. At a gain crossover $|L(j\omega_{\mathrm{gc}})|=1$, the phase margin is $180^\circ+\arg L(j\omega_{\mathrm{gc}})$. Check all relevant crossovers and closed-loop stability before interpreting either margin.4
zero order hold
A zero-order hold keeps each controller output constant until the next sample. With sampling period $T_s$,
$$u_h(t)=u[k],\qquad kT_s\leq t<(k+1)T_s.$$

zero order hold
A zero-order hold keeps each controller output constant until the next sample. With sampling period $T_s$,
$$u_h(t)=u[k],\qquad kT_s\leq t<(k+1)T_s.$$
ZOH discretization matches the continuous plant’s output at the sample times for this held input.5 The sampling rate and Nyquist frequency are
$$f_s=\frac{1}{T_s},\qquad f_N = \frac{1}{2}f_s.$$
To recover a baseband signal without aliasing, its frequency content must lie below $f_N$. A hold does not remove frequencies above this limit; use an anti-aliasing filter before sampling when needed.6
